item.title: Her immigrant parents built a NYC grocery store from scratch. Now Mamdani's experiment could end it
item.description: Josefina Aguirre's Spanish Harlem meat market faces a taxpayer-backed competitor just two blocks away under Zohran Mamdani's municipal grocery plan.
item.content:encoded:
"It's going to be $1," Josefina Aguirre said to a customer, pausing an interview with Fox News Digital inside her family's Spanish Harlem meat market.

"Okay, I'm sorry. I got a couple of customers. Let's start over," Aguirre, a first-generation American, said. "This is me," she added with a laugh from behind the counter where she has worked for the past 30 years.

Aguirre is among the neighborhood grocers suing New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani over his plan to open city-backed grocery stores across all five boroughs. He says the plan will offer shoppers prices roughly 30% lower than comparable retailers. Local business owners argue it will force small local-run stores to shutter.

EXPERTS SCORCH MAMDANI'S GROCERY PLAN AS AN 'ILLUSION' THAT WILL HAVE TAXPAYERS FOOTING THE BILL

"When we heard Mamdani was opening a grocery store where people are gonna save 30%, it scares us because we don't have the money to compete," Aguirre said.

"I mean, we are New Yorkers, we're not scared of competition, we never have been, but when you have a grocery store coming in like this, it could take us out of business."

One of the proposed city-backed stores is set to open next year at La Marqueta, an existing public market just two blocks from Little Mexico, the family business Aguirre's parents opened in 1997. The city is expected to spend roughly $30 million to build the location, putting a taxpayer-backed competitor practically on Aguirre's doorstep.

NYC TAXPAYERS COULD PAY TWICE UNDER MAMDANI'S CITY-OWNED GROCERY STORE PLAN

For generations, bodegas and small grocery stores have been woven into the fabric of New York City neighborhoods, serving customers who often live just blocks away.

Aguirre said the shop, which she now runs with her two sisters, has survived the COVID-19 pandemic, rising rents and competition from big-box retailers such as a nearby Costco. But after nearly three decades in business, Aguirre fears Mamdani's city-run grocery plan could be the setback her family cannot survive.

"If I’m selling a whole chicken for $13, and he’s giving it for $7, they’re gonna buy the $7 chicken," Aguirre said. "Who doesn’t want a 30% discount?"

For Aguirre, the stakes extend well beyond losing customers.

"I pay my mortgage from here. I pay for my kid's tuition. This is what I've been doing for over 30 years. Do I need to start over in a new career?"

Aguirre's concerns are at the heart of a lawsuit brought by a group of New York City grocers challenging Mamdani's plan, which would use public money and city resources to create competitors they argue private businesses cannot realistically match.

NYC GROCERS SOUND ALARM ON MAMDANI'S SUPERMARKET PLAN: 'WE'LL LOSE CUSTOMERS'

Mamdani has committed $70 million to opening five municipal grocery stores, one in each borough, pitching the model as a way to bring down grocery bills for New Yorkers struggling with the rising cost of food. The stores would operate on city-owned property without having to pay rent or property taxes, advantages Mamdani has argued would allow them to offer lower prices.

Independent grocers argue those same taxpayer-backed advantages would leave businesses like Little Mexico competing on an uneven playing field.

Mamdani's grocery push is also an early test of his broader socialist vision for New York, bringing government-run stores into direct competition with private businesses in a city synonymous with capitalism.

FROM FREE BUSES TO CITY-OWNED GROCERY STORES, HERE ARE MAMDANI’S KEY ECONOMIC PROMISES

For Aguirre, however, the fight is more personal.

"This is what my parents left us," Aguirre said. "It'll be sad to see us leave."

But walking away from the business her family has spent nearly three decades building is the last outcome she wants.

"So what will happen next? The next thing would be closing our business, and we don't want to close, we've been here for years," she said.

Mamdani's office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

item.title: Collins lights up internet with response to Dem challenger fathering children with relative: 'Stone cold'
item.description: Susan Collins used a sly rhetorical move to highlight that opponent Troy Jackson fathered two children with his second cousin during a campaign interview.
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, had a sly way of addressing reports that Troy Jackson, her Democratic opponent, fathered two children with his second cousin.

"Well, I'm not going to bring up the fact that the mother of his two children is his second cousin," Collins told a Politico reporter when asked if Jackson’s personal life would be fair game on the campaign trail. "I don’t know whether people know that or not."

"But you just mentioned it," the reporter shot back.

The clip quickly spread across social media as conservatives praised Collins for her political savvy.

TOP DEM OPERATIVE BRUSHES OFF LATEST SCANDAL PLAGUING MAINE SENATE CANDIDATE AS 'SALACIOUS GOSSIP'

Republican political operative Jesse Hunt reacted to a clip of the interview by calling Collins a "silent killer."

"A less-than-2-minute precis of how Susan Collins is as stone-cold a political combatant as the Senate has ever seen," Politico editor Mike DeBonis wrote on X.

National Rifle Association public affairs director and Maine native Justin Davis responded to the clip by predicting that "the upcoming debates are going to be gold." NOTUS reporter Igor Bobic, meanwhile, said that Collins used a "Trump tactic" by bringing up a subject while pretending not to mention it.

"Count Collins out (like everyone did in ‘20) at your own peril," Targeted Victory CCO Matt Gorman posted on X.

"Susan Collins from the top rope on Troy Jackson," GOP communicator Steve Guest posted on X.

Reports about Jackson’s relationship with his second cousin first surfaced in July, when The Maine Wire reported that Jackson and his longtime partner share the same great-grandparents.

MAINE DEMOCRATS CROWN TROY JACKSON AS PLATNER REPLACEMENT AS FRESH SCRUTINY CLOUDS SENATE RESET

"It's truly hysterical how Democrats can't seem to find one normal dude to run for office," conservative commentator Greg Price posted on X, alluding to the fact that Jackson replaced Graham Platner on the ballot in Maine after he terminated his campaign amid a rape allegation.

Other aspects of Jackson’s personal life have come to the forefront of his Senate campaign, including a 1988 police report which claims he assaulted a man at a bar. The report also states that his partner accused him of pushing her around.

Jackson does not dispute that he attacked another man, but strongly denies laying a hand on his partner, who has said she does not recall giving a statement to that effect to the police.

When asked about the police report in August, Collins told Fox News Digital that "he’s the one that needs to respond to the reports. I’m not going to comment on them. But I will say that based on widespread reporting it appears that he struggles to control his temper ... From my perspective, it seems that vetting is very important. We learned the failure of vetting with Graham Platner. But that’s really up to the Democrats."

EMBATTLED MAINE DEMOCRAT DEADLOCKED WITH COLLINS DESPITE CONTROVERSIES IN KEY SENATE RACE, NEW POLL SHOWS

During her interview with Politico, Collins denied that Jackson would necessarily be an easier opponent than Platner, pointing out that the former has a long political record that he can be criticized over — something that Platner lacked as a political outsider.

Jackson has framed the GOP focus on his personal life as a distraction from the issues Mainers actually care about.

"Susan Collins will do anything to distract from the fact that she votes with Trump 96% of the time and has sold out working people in Maine," his campaign previously told Fox News Digital. "Personal attacks on Troy's family are shameful and desperate."

The Jackson campaign did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Wednesday.

Fox News Digital's Paul Steinhauser contributed to this report.

item.title: Kate Middleton’s carefully planned path to the throne revealed as expert says she ‘played the long game’
item.description: Author Christopher Andersen says Kate Middleton is the monarchy's most important asset, crediting her preternatural calm and Diana-like appeal. Simon Vigar also shares how Kate rose as a beloved royal.
item.content:encoded:
Kate Middleton's remarkable rise from middle-class university student to the Princess of Wales wasn't accidental — according to multiple royal experts, it was carefully planned from the very beginning.

Royal author Simon Vigar wrote in "The Four Wives of Windsor" that Prince William's "right-hand man" said Kate believed in "steady progress" as she learned the ropes of royal life, explaining, "We're not going to rush our fences."

"Catherine is no wallflower, somebody told me," Vigar told Fox News Digital. "She's got definite views about things. William obviously trusts her implicitly, and they need people like that. The queen needed Philip. Charles needs Camilla. And William needs Catherine. [And] she's very clever. I reckon she's probably the cleverest of a lot of them."

KATE MIDDLETON IS 'INDISPENSABLE' TO ROYAL FAMILY AS SLIMMED-DOWN MONARCHY FACES MOUNTING PRESSURE: EXPERT

Vigar said that as a newcomer to the royal family, the Princess of Wales was determined to master the role, carefully carving out her place without overshadowing the monarch.

"For instance, they had various charitable interests, ranging from wounded service personnel to early years education and homelessness," Vigar explained. "The person who linked all of those together under the mental wellbeing banner was Catherine. It wasn't Harry or William. She was the one who said, 'Do you know what the common denominator with all of this is? It's mental wellbeing and mental health.'"

"And so, they started a new charity, sort of an umbrella over those," said Vigar. "She will have learned from the other consorts. You're always one step behind, but you're there as a support. If you think something's not quite right, you say it. Catherine's the person that William can trust absolutely implicitly to give him impartial advice."

WATCH: KATE MIDDLETON’S KEY ROLE BEHIND PRINCE WILLIAM REVEALED BY ROYAL AUTHOR

Kate's journey to becoming the Princess of Wales was unlike that of the royal women who came before her.

"It’s a huge social leap that happened with Catherine," said Vigar. "Lady Diana Spencer was a member of the aristocracy. Camilla’s pretty posh, as we say in this country, not quite as posh as Diana, but posh."

"Catherine's middle class," he continued. "Her parents worked very hard. They built their own business. They were able to send their children to private school. ... And it got her to St. Andrews University, where she met William, of course."

The Prince and Princess of Wales married in 2011. Since then, Kate has devoted herself to several charitable causes and organizations focused on early childhood development, mental health, sports and the outdoors, among others.

"I think Kate was born for this role, as odd as that may sound," Christopher Andersen, author of "Kate!," told Fox News Digital. "She has a preternatural calm, a sense of self and confidence that borders on regal. I think she could have stepped into the role as queen-in-waiting back when she was still a student at St. Andrews University. As it turned out, it was William who dragged his feet and gave Kate 10 years to learn the ropes before popping the question."

WATCH: KATE MIDDLETON IS THE MONARCHY'S SECRET WEAPON: AUTHOR

"In many ways, I think there were some in the royal family who were intimidated by Kate's innate grace and charm, not to mention her Diana-like appeal to the general public," said Andersen. "She knew intuitively when to hold back, when to get along and when to stand her ground."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Kate's patience wasn't the only factor working in her favor. Royal experts told Fox News Digital that William's lengthy courtship — once mocked by critics and tabloids — ultimately gave Kate something few royal brides have had: years to observe the monarchy from the outside before officially joining it.

Andersen argued that while critics once questioned why William waited so long to propose, the extended courtship gave Kate valuable time to understand both the institution and the intense public scrutiny that came with it.

"Knives were out from the moment Kate stepped into the spotlight a quarter-century ago," he said. "She had walked a tightrope for years, no doubt about it. But the entire time she had the love and support of her husband. She seemed to understand instinctively that the cardinal rule was not to upstage the monarch."

Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital that, in his view, Kate wasn’t just finding her footing as a royal wife. She was preparing for the biggest job of her life.

"Kate has played the long game because she realizes she will one day be queen to a King William," said Turner. "That training is far more extensive. There has been a steady build of PR power for Kate. It involves wearing the right clothes, manufacturing the right photographs to show a successful queen-in-waiting, as well as a devoted mother."

Kate is expected to play a major role alongside William during this autumn's busy royal calendar. The Sunday Times reported that she may join William in Mumbai, India, for the Earthshot Prize ceremony in November. Fox News Digital reached out to Kensington Palace for comment.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

If confirmed, it would mark Kate's first Earthshot Prize appearance since the 2022 ceremony in Boston, the first held in the U.S. Kate didn't attend the 2023 event in Singapore, staying home to support her eldest son, Prince George, during a week of school exams. She missed the 2024 awards in Cape Town and the 2025 ceremony in Rio de Janeiro as she scaled back public duties following her 2024 cancer diagnosis.

William launched the Earthshot Prize in 2020 to find and highlight solutions to some of the world's biggest environmental challenges.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"Kate and William are determined to shape their own destiny," said Andersen. "They want to be avatars of change. They don't want the monarchy to become so hidebound that it collapses from its own weight. At the same time, they respect tradition and history and aren't about to throw the baby out with the bathwater. They are secure enough now to know they can rewrite the rules when it comes to publicity, pressure and palace expectations."

"Kate is the monarchy's most important asset," he said. "True, she was given plenty of time to learn the ropes. But the truth of the matter is that Kate had it in her from the very beginning."

item.title: DHS directs ICE attorneys to seek early dismissal of legally deficient asylum claims
item.description: DHS is directing ICE attorneys to seek early dismissal of asylum claims deemed legally insufficient, allowing judges to decide them without a full merits hearing.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE – The Department of Homeland Security has issued new guidance directing its immigration attorneys to seek early dismissal of asylum claims they determine are legally insufficient, according to internal guidance obtained by Fox News Digital.

Effective immediately, attorneys with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's (ICE) Office of the Principal Legal Advisor (OPLA) are expected to seek dismissal of asylum applications they determine fail to meet the legal standard on their face by filing motions to pretermit in immigration court.

A motion to pretermit asks an immigration judge to deny an asylum application before a full merits hearing because the government argues the application is legally insufficient. 

Immigration judges ultimately decide whether to grant those motions.

ICE SEEKS NEARLY $500K FINE AGAINST IMMIGRATION LAWYER ACCUSED OF FILING FAKE ASYLUM CLAIMS

The guidance is intended to expedite the adjudication of asylum claims that satisfy the legal requirements while allowing the government to challenge deficient applications earlier in the immigration court process.

The directive also reinforces the administration's ongoing focus on combating asylum fraud, including continued efforts to hold attorneys accountable for facilitating fraudulent asylum claims.

TRUMP ADMIN EYES HISTORIC MASS VISA REVOCATION TARGETING UP TO 200K ASYLUM SEEKERS: REPORT

The policy follows a series of recent administration actions aimed at reshaping the asylum system. Earlier this year, the administration streamlined portions of the affirmative asylum process by allowing certain applications to move directly to immigration court without first undergoing asylum interviews, a change officials said would reduce duplicative reviews and help address the immigration court backlog.

The administration has also expanded its focus on asylum fraud. In recent months, ICE announced a policy allowing the agency to pursue civil penalties against attorneys accused of facilitating fraudulent asylum claims and later sought financial penalties against a New York immigration attorney accused of filing fraudulent asylum applications.

TRUMP SCORES SCOTUS ASYLUM WIN — BUT LIBERAL JUSTICE WARNS IT COULD BACKFIRE AT BORDER

The latest guidance extends that broader effort into immigration court litigation by directing government attorneys to challenge asylum claims they believe do not satisfy the legal requirements before those cases proceed to full evidentiary hearings.

The policy marks another step in the Trump administration's broader effort to tighten the asylum system through changes to immigration enforcement and litigation strategy.

item.title: MAGA begins to crack as 2026 GOP roster backs away from Trump's tech vision
item.description: Donald Trump urges communities to "let Data Reign," but GOP candidates across battleground states propose data center moratoriums ahead of midterms.
item.content:encoded:
With a slew of polls showing that most Americans oppose the construction in their communities of new data centers to power AI, a growing number of Republicans running in this year's elections are putting daylight between themselves and President Donald Trump.

Trump, a strong proponent of data center development, took to social media Monday to argue that if communities "want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign."

But with GOP strategists warning that data centers have become politically radioactive, some Republicans on the midterm ballot are reversing course, which is a stark shift for a party that previously had fully embraced the burgeoning AI industry.

Seventy percent of voters questioned in a recent Fox News poll said they wanted to hit the brakes on building data centers in their area to support artificial intelligence, with only 30% in favor. Only 40% of Republicans, and 46% of MAGA Republicans supported new data center construction.

CRUCIAL SENATE RACE ERUPTS OVER AI'S MASSIVE ENERGY APPETITE

Fueling the opposition are concerns over rising electricity costs and energy and water consumption.

"I think we need to take a pause, probably, and make sure that we're answering all the questions that people have on them," former Rep. Mike Rogers, the GOP Senate nominee in battleground Michigan, said two weeks ago when asked about data center construction.

Rogers, who previously welcomed data center expansion in Michigan, later outlined a one-year moratorium, arguing that "Michigan needs stronger guardrails to protect community control, prevent utility price hikes, protect our water, and stop pay-to-play schemes."

DEMOCRAT FETTERMAN ALIGNS WITH TRUMP ON AI ARGUMENT

He's far from alone.

In Ohio's crucial Senate race between appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted and his Democratic challenger, former longtime Sen. Sherrod Brown, the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) warned that the issue could help the Democrats flip the seat. Brown and allied groups have shelled out millions of dollars to run ads calling Husted "the face of data centers in Ohio."

"More than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck," the NRSC memo emphasized.

Husted has introduced a Senate bill to stop average Americans from paying for data center energy costs.

BERNIE SANDERS: 'WE MUST HIT THE PAUSE ON AI BEFORE IT'S TOO LATE'

The political pushback stretches well beyond Michigan and Ohio.

Texas Attorney General and U.S. Senate nominee Ken Paxton last month unveiled a four-point plan to curb rapid data center growth and address public concerns over resource strain.  

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican running for a fourth term steering the Lone Star State, halted new data center connections to the state's power grid pending a comprehensive regulatory audit.

Ohio Republican gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy pledged to issue a first-day-in-office executive order halting approval of all new data center projects until his proposed safeguards are enacted.

Rep. Tom Tiffany, the GOP nominee for governor in swing state Wisconsin, has highlighted that he opposes new data centers unless strict conditions are met. Tiffany has made data centers a centerpiece of his gubernatorial campaign, slamming his Democratic rival, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, as "Data Center David Crowley."

Pennsylvania Treasurer and Republican gubernatorial nominee Stacy Garrity has called for a temporary pause on new and uncontracted major data center developments in her battleground state.

Other Republicans are stopping short of moratoriums. Rep. Byron Donalds, the GOP gubernatorial nominee who opposes bans or moratoriums and whose primary campaign received significant backing from the AI industry, introduced legislation this summer that would require large AI data centers to generate their own power and water rather than draw from public utilities.

COOL YOUR SERVERS: CHECK OUT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POLL ON AI DATA CENTERS

Trump is standing firm.

The president recently called Abbott's decision to pump the brakes on data center development a "mistake."

And Trump, on Monday said, "If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame."

The president, who has made data centers a key ingredient in winning the AI race with China, argued: "China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement."

But Trump, at least for now, seems to be giving Republicans some wiggle room.

"If a Republican’s against a data center, that’s OK with me," Trump said.

Veteran Republican strategist Matt Gorman told Fox News Digital that "Trump is smartly taking the long view of this."

Gorman said "Republicans on the ballot this year are being responsive to the very real concerns people have," adding that "these companies and their champions have to do more to make the case."

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

The AI industry is responding to the political backlash.

Build American AI, an industry-aligned group powered by top AI leaders, this week launched a multimillion-dollar public engagement campaign to build support for "clear, strong, and commonsense policies governing the development of the data centers and energy infrastructure."

It highlighted that the "policies should protect residential ratepayers, safeguard the environment and water resources, require developers to pay their fair share, and preserve the right of every community to decide whether it wants to welcome data center investment."

"We can protect ratepayers, safeguard our natural resources, respect the right of communities to decide whether they want to welcome this investment, and still build the infrastructure America needs to lead the world in artificial intelligence," Build American AI added.

item.title: Johnson downplays GOP's midterm woes as Democrats eye House takeover: 'I am very bullish'
item.description: With Election Day two months away, Democrats eye Senate and House majorities as inflation, gas prices and Trump's approval ratings batter the GOP.
item.content:encoded:
With two months to go until Election Day, and early voting kicking off later this month in half a dozen states, Democrats are increasingly optimistic they can recapture congressional majorities.

With the final stretch towards the midterms underway, Democrats see an unexpectedly favorable political environment despite their own weak national brand, while Republicans insist structural advantages and the Democrats' shift to the left will allow them to defy midterm history.

Senate Republicans control their chamber by a 53-47 margin, and the majority is even more fragile in the House. And the latest forecasts from the leading nonpartisan political handicappers keep leaning towards the Democrats.

But a defiant House Speaker Mike Johnson not only predicts the GOP will hold control of the chamber, but he tells Fox News Digital, "We're going to grow the majority."

SPEAKER JOHNSON'S MIDTERM PREDICTION TO BUCK HISTORY

Republicans — as the party currently in power — were already up against traditional political headwinds that have historically led to a loss of congressional seats during midterm election years. Add to that the challenging climate fueled by persistent inflation Americans see daily at the grocery store, high gas prices tied to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran and President Donald Trump's well underwater approval ratings.

"We are going to take back the Senate. Republicans thought they had the Senate locked down, but now Democrats, we are on the path to victory. We've blown the map wide open," longtime Senate Democratic Leader Sen. Chuck Schumer of New York told reporters two weeks ago.

But Democrats have problems of their own as they try to win back control of congressional majorities in the midterms, including a party brand that public opinion polling indicates is extremely unpopular. And high-profile victories this spring and summer by left-wing and socialist candidates over establishment rivals in Democratic primaries are giving Republicans extra ammunition to portray all Democrats as extremists.

THESE 12 MIDTERM RACES WILL DECIDE WHICH PARTY CONTROLS THE SENATE

"It's a contrast election, and people are making a contrast between common-sense solutions and candidates, and really crazy, which is represented by the other side," Johnson claimed, during a Fox News Digital interview on the campaign trail in Maine. "I am very bullish about the outcome on election night."

In the battle for the House, the mid-decade redistricting push by Trump and GOP leaders is giving Republicans a boost, with a potential net gain of up to a dozen newly drawn right-tilting districts across the country.

But in a sign of the rough landscape facing the GOP, House Democrats last month expanded their midterm target list to 58 Republican-held districts, including 12 seats in territory Trump carried in 2024.

The victories by Trump and Republicans two years ago were fueled by Americans fed up with the high cost of living. Two years later, inflation is the Republicans' biggest liability.

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Three out of four voters questioned in the most recent Fox News national poll said inflation had caused financial hardship, while 54% expected the economy to worsen.

The Fox News poll and other recent surveys also indicate Democrats holding an enthusiasm advantage over Republicans, and continuing to lead on the generic ballot question, which asks if a respondent would vote for the Democrat or Republican in their congressional district without offering specific names.

"Donald Trump started a war that no one wanted, and now Americans are paying the price. Gas prices are soaring and families who were already struggling in Trump’s economy are forced to stretch their budgets even further while footing the bill for this war," Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin said in a statement.

Republicans hold a campaign cash edge over Democrats, and remain optimistic about the midterms.

"We have a chance to defy history and win the midterms," Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Joe Gruters told Fox News Digital this summer.

Gruters and other GOP leaders are spotlighting the major tax cuts on tips, overtime and Social Security that congressional Republicans passed and Trump signed into law last year.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

But Republicans are facing a low-propensity problem: MAGA voters who don't always go to the polls when Trump's name isn't on the ballot.

Gruters called Trump the "best showman that's ever existed in politics, bar none... He knows how to deliver these low-propensity voters. He knows how to get people up, motivated, excited about the midterms, and that's what we're going to need."

And he pointed to next week's first ever GOP midterm convention and said, "It gives us a chance to highlight all the wonderful things this president has done in our effort on this great American comeback."

But Democrats are touting their own get-out-the-vote efforts.

"This year, the DNC organizing team launched Local Listeners, a first-of-its-kind program that talked to nearly 10,000 people who voted in 2020, but not 2024," the DNC's Martin said. "What we found could change the game for the midterms this year."

item.title: MORNING GLORY: 'Blue Blight' is spreading fast and only voters can stop it
item.description: Manufacturing jobs, gas prices and college enrollment are declining in blue states as "blue blight" spreads, reshaping where students choose to live.
item.content:encoded:
"Blue blight" is spreading across northeastern and west coast America, with scattered outbreaks in the interior of the country like Illinois and Colorado. It is up to voters to stop its spread.

"Blue blight" isn’t a term-of-art yet. But, it will be.

Consider that Dutch Elm Disease wasn’t a term familiar to Americans in the 1920s either. The devastating fungus arrived in the United States in the early 1930s and notably impacted a handful of Elm trees in Cleveland, Ohio. By the end of the 1970s, the Elms that had defined the Courthouse Square of my hometown of Warren as well as my own street, and, indeed, all of northeast Ohio were almost all gone. The fungus spread far and wide beyond Ohio, leaving a trail of felled tree stumps in its wake. To this day, it remains a threat to the remaining Elm population in the United States, even after it killed three out of four Elms across the country, and almost all of them in some places like northeastern Ohio.

CALIFORNIA CONTROLLER CANDIDATE SLAMS MASSIVE EDUCATION SPENDING DESPITE WORSE STUDENT RESULTS

The impacts of "blue blight" are becoming as visible as that of Dutch Elm Disease. Those impacts are most noticeable, to cite just two examples, in decreases in the quality of public education and declines in manufacturing jobs, even as state and local taxes rise. The second order impacts are now being felt across universities and colleges in states that are considered "blue."

Kudos to The Wall Street Journal’s Douglas Belkin and Roshan Fernandez for their August 29 article titled "Why Syracuse Can’t Attract the Students It Needs to Pay the Bills."

Kudos as well to Mary Katharine Ham and Vic Matus of the "Getting Hammered" podcast for some interesting speculation, prompted by the work of Belkin and Fernandez, on how the smaller number of college students — just the demographics of the decade ahead — are going to be looking beyond their choice of college to the job market and cost-of-living in the area surrounding their future campus and factoring those variables into their enrollment decision. Ham and Matus commented that perhaps students are going to tilt south to states like Florida rather than north to New York if they are looking at life choices ahead.

Life choices as in "here are the jobs" and "what’s it cost to live in that state long term?"

THE REAL REASON AMERICANS ARE FLEEING BLUE STATES FOR FLORIDA AND TEXAS

I checked the numbers that are available against their thesis and, indeed, the available stats back them up.

Using the data available from the Department of Education’s National Center for Education Statistics for the years 2017-2022 (the latest available) "blue states" — those that voted for then Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 — experienced substantially faster enrollment decline in higher ed than red states.

NEW YORK CITY'S DECLINING PUBLIC SCHOOL ENROLLMENT PROJECTED TO LOSE OVER 150K MORE AS POPULATION DECLINES

Of the six states that saw enrollments rise in their colleges and universities, five are "red": Georgia, Kentucky, Arizona, Indiana and Utah. Some deep red states did poorly (Alaska and Iowa) but the overall trend is there.

Another factor to check on: manufacturing jobs.

CEO SAYS DOING BUSINESS IN STATE ‘SUCKS’ AS COMPANY HEADS TO TEXAS AMID CALIFORNIA EXODUS

When I first moved to California in 1978, its population was about 22 million souls and the state was home to close to 2 million manufacturing jobs. The Golden State’s population is today a half million shy of 40 million, but its total of manufacturing jobs has not simply failed to keep up with the population growth; the number of manufacturing jobs has actually plummeted to 1.2 million.

How does that happen? "Blue blight."

Another data point. California had 23 refineries in 2000. It is home to 11 today. Over 40 years, the refining output in the state has dropped by a million barrels a day. California motorists are paying about far more per gallon than red state residents. The cost in Indiana is several dollars a gallon cheaper. "Blue blight" claims victims in many ways but nowhere more than among those who consume energy.

Voters get the laws and regulations they vote for, and they can change or stay the course their home states are on. No doubt some citizens prefer the blue abyss ahead for high tax/high regulation states. But all voters get to choose. And they get to change their minds if the spread of "blue blight" alarms them.

item.title: The cure for socialism is giving more Americans a stake in capitalism
item.description: Socialism is gaining ground because fewer Americans are homeowners and stockholders, creating a perfect opening for DSA leaders like Zohran Mamdani.
item.content:encoded:
With each passing election, the socialist surge is rising. Bernie Sanders-backed Abdul El-Sayed won the Michigan Democratic Senate primary, defeating a well-funded establishment candidate. In Wisconsin, Francesca Hong — a democratic socialist who once called for canceling Thanksgiving — came within 3,000 votes of winning her state's gubernatorial primary. The DSA darling Zohran Mamdani is already the mayor of America’s largest city.

Some argue that socialism has hit its high-water mark and is losing momentum. Count me skeptical. Socialism is gaining ground because, for too many, capitalism has become a spectator sport. The biggest reason more voters support state ownership is that fewer people are owners themselves.

Consider the numbers. The national homeownership rate sits at 65% — down from a peak of 69.2% in 2004 and below the 25-year average. Among Americans under 35, it has fallen to just 35.2%, down more than a percentage point from a year ago. The generational gap is stark: Just 57% of Americans in their mid-30s own homes today compared to 64% of their parents' generation at the same age. With the 30-year mortgage rate recently climbing 6.69%, the homeownership rate is not about to improve anytime soon.

BILLIONS SPENT BY KEY FEDERAL AGENCY HASN'T MADE AMERICAN DREAM OF HOMEOWNERSHIP ANY EASIER: REPORT

The picture is similar in financial markets. Sixty-two percent of Americans own stock — but that number conceals the real story. Only 28% of households earning under $50,000 own any stock at all; for those with only a high school education or less, it's 42%, and for those 18 to 29, it’s 44%.

Declining ownership rates create a perfect opportunity for the far left. People with property don’t like the government taking it. People without ownership see government-sponsored theft as more acceptable. Because it’s not state ownership that invigorates voters, but the promise that they too can share in the wealth of society.

THE NUMBERS DON’T LIE. YOUNG AMERICANS ARE FALLING IN LOVE … WITH SOCIALISM

This puts into perspective policies like Mamdani’s rent freeze — a false antidote to the difficulty of owning a home in New York. Rent freezes promise that people can stay in their apartments and the market cannot move them out. Likewise, when Sanders touts legislation to give the government a 50% stake in AI companies, it makes people feel like they have a stake in America’s biggest companies even if they don’t actually own a single stock.

Yet these policies attempt to address symptoms while worsening the disease. A rent freeze may let you stay in an apartment owned by somebody else, but it proactively prevents actual ownership by reducing supply, degrading building quality and making conditions worse. And a government stake in AI companies may well flood the coffers of the IRS. But that does nothing to give actual people a stake in the success of high-growth companies.

EL-SAYED REVEALS HE WOULD GO ‘STEP FURTHER’ THAN SANDERS ON SOCIALIST PLAN FOR MAJOR US INDUSTRY

Still, however true these arguments are, they aren’t persuading voters. The most effective answer to Mamdani and the Democratic Socialists of America is not to point out the problems with socialism — it’s to give people an actual stake in society by increasing the number of homeowners and shareholders who have an interest in America’s success.

Founders and employees with skin in the game think longer term. They protect customers, watch costs, solve problems and weather downturns differently because the outcome is partly theirs. They certainly don’t appreciate heavy-handed government.

And while not everyone is called to be a business owner, nearly everyone can be a homeowner. Business coalitions should be pushing cities to permit more housing, shorten approval times and clear the regulatory barriers that make construction expensive. Companies can complement those efforts with matched savings programs, closing-cost assistance and financial coaching for first-time buyers.

As AI threatens corporate headcounts, empowers small business development and accelerates the pandemic-induced emptying of downtown office buildings, we can also convert surplus commercial space into residential units. Adaptive reuse avoids the embodied carbon of demolition and new construction — and buildings account for nearly 37% of total U.S. energy consumption. Bringing underutilized commercial space back to productive residential use is one of the most practical emissions reductions available in the built environment, delivering a housing win and a climate win simultaneously.

AMERICA’S BROKEN PERMITTING SYSTEM IS QUIETLY RAISING YOUR COST OF LIVING

The path to stock ownership needs to be widened too. Broad-based equity compensation — stock grants, profit-sharing, employee stock ownership plans — can turn workers into partners in growth. Automatic retirement enrollment, meaningful employer matching and access to low-cost diversified investments can give workers a stake in American prosperity even before they can afford a home, especially if those investments are tied to high-growth fields like artificial intelligence or clean energy.

None of this requires turning companies into charities. It is capitalism with aligned incentives — workers who accumulate assets, communities that keep their employers and a free-enterprise system defended by people protecting something they actually own.

The DSA sells government control because too many Americans believe the private economy has no place for them. The strongest defense of capitalism is opening a credible path for people to not only find their place, but to own it.

item.title: Pessimists say the economy is weak. The good news is, they are wrong
item.description: Trump tax reforms sparked $296 billion in IRS refunds along with new deductions for qualified tips and overtime pay rewarding working Americans.
item.content:encoded:
The pessimists are wrong, and the numbers prove it.

While a chorus of commentators insists the American economy is faltering, businesses are seeing strong returns — and investing those dollars to grow. From record-breaking tax refunds this spring to surging business investment across every sector, the evidence of economic strength is overwhelming for anyone willing to look past the headlines.

American businesses aren't just investing — they're going on offense. Companies are purchasing equipment, upgrading technology, modernizing facilities and hiring people. They're planning for growth, not bracing for decline. And thanks to the Trump administration's tax reforms, they finally have the certainty and the incentives to put capital to work right now.

WHITE HOUSE ECONOMIST PROJECTS GDP GROWTH COULD TOP 5% AMID CAPITAL SPENDING BOOM

The One Big Beautiful Bill fundamentally changed the game. For entrepreneurs still sitting on the sidelines, the message couldn't be clearer: stop waiting. This is the year to invest. Every month you delay is a month your competitors are pulling ahead, taking advantage of provisions designed to reward exactly the kind of bold investment that builds lasting success.

Consider what's happened. The permanent restoration of 100% bonus depreciation lets businesses recover the full cost of qualifying investments immediately — not over years. That means a manufacturer can purchase new machinery, a restaurant can renovate its kitchen or a tech startup can upgrade its servers, and every one of them can deduct the full cost in the same tax year.

TRUMP'S TAX CUTS HAND REPUBLICANS A KILLER ARGUMENT FOR THE MIDTERMS

Section 179 has been expanded, letting small businesses deduct even more upfront. The IRS has even issued guidance to make the path clearer and give owners the confidence to move forward without hesitation.

Now look at what happened this spring. A Government Accountability Office report released Aug. 10 shows the IRS issued $296 billion in refunds during the 2026 filing season — a 17% jump from the previous year. That's $43 billion more flowing back into Americans' pockets.

REPUBLICANS BET HIGHER TAX REFUNDS WILL BOOST MIDTERM CHANCES AS BLUE STATES RESIST RELIEF

The average refund rose by $333, and the IRS processed more than 8 million additional refunds. The GAO attributed this surge, in part, to millions claiming new deductions created by the law — including provisions for qualified tips and overtime pay.

Let that sink in. Working Americans — waitresses, factory workers, overtime earners — are keeping more of what they earn because this tax code finally rewards work instead of punishing it. That's not a talking point. That's real money in real people's bank accounts. Money that gets spent at local restaurants, invested in home improvements, saved for college tuition and plowed back into the communities where these families live and work.

TRUMP HITS KEY BATTLEGROUNDS TO SELL TAX CUTS, BOOST GOP AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

The critics who keep telling you the economy is weak need to explain why businesses keep expanding. Why entrepreneurs keep taking risks. Why companies keep investing in productivity, hiring and growth. The answer is simple: they see opportunity. They see an economy gaining momentum, not losing it. While the doomsayers scroll through bad headlines, business owners are reading their balance sheets — and what they see is encouraging enough to act.

The Trump administration delivered tax policies that reward investment, protect working families and let Americans keep more of what they earn. When business owners know they can recover investment costs immediately, they act. When workers see bigger refunds because the tax code now values their tips and overtime, they spend, save and reinvest in their own futures and in their local economies.

LIZ PEEK: THE TRUMP ECONOMY IS DOING BETTER THAN THE MEDIA WANT TO ADMIT

Tax relief doesn't just sound good on paper. It translates directly into growth. The proof is in every business owner putting capital on the line right now — and in the billions returned to American taxpayers this year. When a company buys new equipment, expands a facility, hires another worker or opens another location, that's not speculation. That's commitment. That's confidence made visible.

The law also strengthens incentives for domestic innovation by allowing qualifying research and development expenditures to be deducted immediately. That means companies aren't just investing in what they already do — they're investing in what comes next. Favorable treatment for qualified production property gives manufacturers another reason to build here, expand here and hire here. America is open for business, and the tax code now reflects that reality.

The businesses I work with aren't retreating. They're expanding. They're hiring. They're investing for the long term. That's not what a weak economy looks like. That's what an economy preparing to roar looks like.

Anyone still calling this economy weak isn’t paying attention to the right indicators.

item.title: DOJ threatens to cut billions in welfare funding from states for failing to report illegal migrants
item.description: The Justice Department warns states they could lose billions in welfare funding if they fail to report illegal immigrants to DHS under new rules.
item.content:encoded:
The Justice Department warned states they could lose billions of dollars in welfare funding if they do not report known illegal migrants to the federal government, according to a legal opinion released Wednesday.

The DOJ's Office of Legal Counsel said states participating in two key welfare programs must require all state agencies to report individuals known to be unlawfully present to the Department of Homeland Security, a significant shift that the administration says will help enforce President Donald Trump's crackdown on illegal immigration. The opinion reverses a 1998 Office of Legal Counsel interpretation that limited the reporting requirement to agencies administering the programs.

Previously, only the state agencies that administered the funding for the welfare programs were required to report illegal migrants, while other state agencies that might be aware of these individuals, including colleges and departments of motor vehicles, were not subject to this mandate.

DHS BOSS REVEALS OVAL OFFICE PLAN TO 'WITHHOLD FUNDING' FROM SANCTUARY CITIES AFTER AGGRESSIVE NEW YORK BUST

"Failure to comply may lead to serious consequences, including loss of program funding," Deputy Assistant Attorney General Joshua Craddock said in a statement.

Since returning to the White House, Trump has taken an aggressive approach targeting both illegal and legal immigration.

The president's crackdown on illegal immigration has included deploying federal agents into cities across the country to conduct raids on migrant communities and increasingly partnering with state and local law enforcement and outside companies to locate suspected illegal migrants.

DOJ ACCUSES MARYLAND OF 'ACTIVE AND DELIBERATE EFFORT' TO PREVENT DEPORTATIONS OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS: LAWSUIT

The administration has repeatedly attempted to pressure Democrat-led states that have refused cooperation with federal immigration enforcement, including by threatening federal funding.

The shift could face legal challenges. Democrat-led states have already sued to block DHS from collecting personal details of people receiving funds under one of the programs, Temporary Assistance for Needy Families.

Courts have also limited some administration efforts to require the sharing of information on migrants with DHS. But in some cases, judges allowed federal immigration authorities to collect certain information, including Medicaid data.

All 50 states and Washington, D.C., participate in the reporting requirements tied to the two programs: Temporary Assistance for Needy Families and Supplemental Security Income.

Federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Families grants exceed $16.5 billion annually, and Supplemental Security Income federal benefits exceed $60 billion annually.

Illegal migrants are not eligible for either program.

Reuters contributed to this report.
